name: Question 11
problem: Suppose that a matrix $A$ has characteristic polynomial $p(\lambda )=(\lambda +2)(\lambda -5)^{19},$ the rank of $(A-5I)^{5}$ equals $12,$ and the rank of $(A-5I)^{6}$ equals $9.$ If a basis of ${R}^{20}$ consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of $A$, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank $6$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =5?$
worked_solution:
For the given matrix $A$ with eigenvalue $\lambda =5,$ a generalized eigenvector of rank $6$ is a vector $v$ such that 

$$
(A-5I)^{6}v=0\,\text{and}\,(A-5I)^{5}v\ne 0.
$$

Notice that $A$ must be a $20\times 20$ matrix.

- Since the rank of $(A-5I)^{5}$ equals $12,$ then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

$$
\text{nullity}(A-5I)^{5}=20-12=8.
$$

So, the solutions to $(A-5I)^{5}v=0$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{5}$ of dimension $8$ in ${R}^{20}.$

- Since the rank of $(A-5I)^{6}$ equals $9,$  then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that

$$
\text{nullity}(A-5I)^{6}=20-9=11.
$$

So, the solutions to $(A-5I)^{6}v=0$ form a subspace $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{6}$ of dimension $11$ in ${R}^{20}.$

Since $\text{Null}(A-2I)^{5}$ is a subspace of dimension $8$ in $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{6}$, which is a subspace of dimension $11,$ our basis can contain only $3$ vectors that lie in $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{6}$ but do not lie in $\text{Null}(A-5I)^{5}.$

Therefore, there will be 

$$
\text{nullity}(A-5I)^{6}-\text{nullity}(A-5I)^{5}=11-8=3
$$

 generalized eigenvectors of rank $6$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =5.$

If a basis of R20 consists of linearly independent generalized eigenvectors of A, how many of these are generalized eigenvectors of rank 6 corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=5?

EXPLANATION

For the given matrix A with eigenvalue λ=5, a generalized eigenvector of rank 6 is a vector v such that

(A−5I)6v=0and(A−5I)5v≠0.

Notice that A must be a 20×20 matrix.

  • Since the rank of (A−5I)5 equals 12, then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that nullity(A−5I)5=20−12=8. So, the solutions to (A−5I)5v=0 form a subspace Null(A−5I)5 of dimension 8 in R20.

  • Since the rank of (A−5I)6 equals 9, then by the rank-nullity theorem, we have that nullity(A−5I)6=20−9=11. So, the solutions to (A−5I)6v=0 form a subspace Null(A−5I)6 of dimension 11 in R20.

Since Null(A−2I)5 is a subspace of dimension 8 in Null(A−5I)6, which is a subspace of dimension 11, our basis can contain only 3 vectors that lie in Null(A−5I)6 but do not lie in Null(A−5I)5.

Therefore, there will be nullity(A−5I)6−nullity(A−5I)5=11−8=3 generalized eigenvectors of rank 6 corresponding to the eigenvalue λ=5.
